newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Mark tumbles on Euro crosses, Norway shines.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mark tumbles on Euro crosses, Norway shines.

text.p: The mark weakened sharply on many of its European crosses on Friday, plunging to its lowest level against the Norwegian crown for more than four years and eroding key levels against the peseta.

The backdrop of weak German economic data released on Thursday helped to push the mark lower, while the apparent halting of intervention by the central banks of Norway and Spain sped up the decline, analysts said.
Many European countries have been locked in a struggle to prevent their currencies from appreciating further in order to avoid losing export competitiveness.
"As it is, the central banks of Norway and Spain appear to have given up the fight for the time being," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London.
But several other central banks were said to have jumped to the mark's defence in European morning trading as its weakness gathered momentum.

Dealers said the Bank of Finland sold markkas for marks, while the Bank of Portugal was seen buying marks for escudos. The Swedish Riksbank was also rumoured to have intervened in the market to slow the decline of the mark/Swedish crown rate.

The mark's slide accelerated after the Norwegian central bank said it would not intervene in the currency market for some time. It had been an aggressive seller of the crown recently to stem its appreciation, traders said.
The mark/Norwegian crown rate fell to a low of 4.03 per mark before recovering to 4.0470/10 by midsession. At the start of this week the crown stood around 4.13 per mark.
The crown is subject to a "dirty float", which means that the central bank intervenes to maintain a level that is not declared officially.
Announcing a temporary policy shift, the Norwegian bank said it would not intervene to any substantial extent in the foreign exchange market over a period.

The crown's surge forced the central bank to cut official interest rates for the second time this week, lowering the deposit and overnight rates by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.25 and 5.25 percent, respectively.
The Norwegian central bank said it had sold a cumulative 20 billion crowns ($3.1 billion) since the start of 1997.
Dealers said the mark/peseta rate fell through the key 84 peseta level as the Bank of Spain, which had been defending the mark heavily against the peseta since Wednesday, pulled its bids.
The Spanish central bank had been defending the 84 level for several months, they said. Its currency reserves have swollen considerably and rose by $1.64 billion in December to $61.83 billion.

The Norwegian crown has become a favourite for foreign exchange traders attracted by the solid fundamentals of the Norwegian economy, such as its huge, oil-related current account and fiscal surpluses, analysts said.
The recent rise in oil prices has been a boon for the crown as Norway is a key oil producer and exporter.
"There is a lot on the plus side for the Norwegian crown and a lot of investors are waking up to that," said Norfield.
The weak mark theme was reinforced by German data released on Thursday.

"It's not solely a Norwegian crown story," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London. "The weak German data helped revive speculation that German interest rates will be cut again."
German unemployment rose by 48,000 in December to 4.156 million, or 10.8 percent of the workforce.
Gross domestic product data reinforced perceptions that the German economy would remain in the doldrums for quite some time.
GDP rose by 1.4 percent last year after 1.9 percent growth in 1995. The economy stagnated in the final quarter with virtually no growth from the third quarter.
-- London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792 ($1=6.396 Norwegian Crown)
